Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. (Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.)

1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025
Net debt inflows from official creditors decreased 19.6 percent to $30.3 billion in 2025, a consequence of the decline in official bilateral and multilateral net debt inflows. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. Official creditors, including the Group of Seven (G-7) bilateral creditors and multilaterals like the European Union and the World Bank Group, provided $122.2 billion in disbursements during the 2022–25 period. This support reshaped the composition of Ukraine’s external debt (figure B1.4.1). Long-term external debt stock rose from $99 billion in 2015 to $227 billion in 2025, but little of that increase was driven by private creditors, whose claims remained broadly flat over the past decade, rising slightly from $72 billion to $82 billion. Debt owed to multilateral creditors accounts for most of the increase. Bilateral claims increased sixfold over the past decade but grew from a much smaller base and remained a modest share of the total. These official creditors delivered support to Ukraine not only through direct lending but also through grants, trust funds, guarantees, and co- and parallel financing, among other financial instruments.

LMICs’ debt stock owed to all other creditor groups also increased in 2025. Debt stock owed to official creditors (public institutions such as national governments and international organizations) increased 8.4 percent in 2025, to $2.0 trillion. Lending by official bilateral creditors (national governments and their agencies) also showed a comeback, increasing 4.7 percent in 2025 after a 3.4 percent retrenchment in 2024. Support from multilateral institutions such as the World Bank Group and the IMF continued to be positive in 2025, but at a decreasing pace when compared to the COVID-19 pandemic era. Except for the multilateral support to Ukraine provided under the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration Loans for Ukraine initiative, the cumulative countercyclical lending by these institutions decelerated in 2025. (Box 1.4 describes the international support for Ukraine through this initiative.) LMICs’ debt stock owed to multilateral creditors increased 9.6 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. However, when the European Union’s support to Ukraine is excluded, debt stock owed to multilateral creditors increased 7.0 percent to $1.4 trillion in 2026.

This behavior is even more evident at the creditor composition level. In 2025, multilateral institutions continued to provide positive support, a trend that has continued since 2007. Net transfers from these institutions increased 36.4 percent in 2025, rebounding from the downward trend recorded since 2022, following the COVID-19 extraordinary financing. During 2025, multilateral institutions provided $21.0 billion more in financing than they received in principal and interest payments. This increase was led by the European Union’s unprecedented support to Ukraine, with the organization providing $32.6 billion more to LMICs than it received in 2025. The World Bank Group was the second-largest provider of net transfers to LMICs during the year, delivering $3.5 billion more than it received. Net transfers to LMICs from bilateral creditors were negative for the second year in a row, though at an improving pace, with this creditor base receiving $3.4 billion more than it provided in 2025.
